claims.evidence: Role swaps, reversed order and a rewired edge all change the encoding; without the relevant operator, the encodings are identical.
claims.boundary: Controlled pairs confirm the design; they do not show general graph reasoning.

claims.evidence: 96.3% precision@5 against 25.0% for random ranking. All 9,000 top results trace to source records and reconstruct their scores exactly.
claims.boundary: No non-HDC retrieval baseline. Ablation gains partly reflect how the patterns are defined. Contributions are not causes.

claims.evidence: HDC learns most efficiently when labels are scarce: with 1 review per class, it scores 7.4–8.9 points higher macro F1 than LR and the MLP. From 5 reviews per class, the three are on par.
claims.boundary: The advantage shrinks to parity as reviews accumulate.

claims.evidence: Fixed encoder; each delayed review is added in place and can be reversed exactly. 96.7% correct in the delayed-feedback replay.
claims.boundary: Still supervised: labels are required, and an individual update can make predictions worse.

claims.evidence: HDC learns from one new review in 0.130 ms, versus 3.726 ms (LR) and 39.7 ms (MLP) for full retraining. All three predict in at most 0.104 ms.
claims.boundary: One retraining run can absorb a whole batch, so large batches narrow or reverse the gap for LR. Incremental LR/MLP optimizers, energy and production serving were not measured.

claims.evidence: 16,384 bytes per raw hypervector versus 84 bytes per LR/MLP input vector.
claims.boundary: HDC costs more storage here; the float16 search copy halves it without measurable loss.
